summary: This memo reports measurements of round-trip times in the Internet and suggests improvements to how TCP computes its retransmission timeout. It serves as both a status report on the Internet and advice to TCP implementers.

eli5.summary: Someone timed how long messages take to travel and back, then said that the wait before sending again should be chosen more carefully.

questions: how does tcp choose retransmission timeout
how does tcp choose the retransmission timeout
does packet length affect network delay
subtitle: 1983 round-trip measurements across the Internet, and a tweak to TCP's retransmission timeout.

tldr.problem: TCP's retransmission-timeout algorithm needs good parameters, but they had not been tested on real long, lossy Internet paths.
tldr.mechanism: D.L. Mills measured delays with ICMP Echo and Reply messages from a Fuzzball host, simulated the timeout algorithm on the data, and tried using two smoothing weights instead of one.
tldr.outcome: Delay depends on packet length, and using F1 = 15/16 and F2 = 3/4 with G = 2 improved efficiency, by about ten percent on some paths and five percent on most.

today: RFC 889 is an Informational report from December 1983, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It records measurements and advice to TCP implementers; see RFC 793 for the TCP specification it discusses.

sections.title: The Experiments and the Measurement Host
sections.content:
RFC 889 reports two series of experiments run in October and November 1983. One measured network delay against packet length. The other tested the TCP retransmission-timeout algorithm from the standards documents. The goals were to collect benchmark data on real Internet paths and to use it to improve individual TCP implementations.

The measurements came from a Fuzzball, an LSI-11 running IP/TCP plus TELNET, FTP and SMTP. It ran the original PING (Packet InterNet Groper) program, which sent ICMP Echo messages and recorded elapsed times. Test hosts spanned the ARPANET, MILNET, MINET, SATNET, TELENET and many local nets.
sections.eli5: He sent thousands of tiny test messages to computers around the world and wrote down how long each one took to come back.

sections.title: Packet Length Versus Delay
sections.content:
Each run consisted of 512 ICMP Echo/Reply volleys, with lengths drawn uniformly between zero and 256 and anything under 40 rounded up to 40, the minimum for an ICMP message with timestamps and the minimum TCP segment size. Elapsed time was normalized to one-way delay.

On ARPANET paths the data showed two characteristics: one for single-packet messages shorter than 126 octets and one for longer, multi-packet messages. Linear regression lines were fitted to each, and the results are given in a table of delays and computed rates for dozens of hosts.

The data showed a strong correlation between delay and length, with the longest packets delayed two to three times as long as the shortest. Mills advises implementers that some dependency on packet length may be needed in the timeout calculation for lossy nets like SATNET, and that some paths may need timeouts ranging to many seconds. He also observed that delays from ARPANET to MILNET hosts were in the same ballpark as to SATNET hosts, and that MILNET loss was not negligible (18 in 512 for ISIA-2).
sections.eli5: Big messages took two or three times longer than small ones, so a patient sender should wait longer for a big message.

sections.title: The Retransmission-Timeout Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm, sometimes called the RSRE Algorithm, records the time a segment is sent and measures how long its sequence number takes to be acknowledged. It smooths these samples into an estimate of round-trip delay and sets a timeout; if the timeout expires, the segment is resent. Poor parameters mean either wasted retransmissions or slow recovery.

The specified form is a first-order linear recursive filter with a weighting factor F and a threshold factor G. For each delay sample R the estimator is updated as E = F*E + (1 - F)*R, and a packet is retransmitted if an interval of G*E expires. The specification suggested F of 0.8 to 0.9 and G of 1.5 to 2.0.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps a running guess of how long a reply takes, then waits a bit longer than that guess before assuming the message was lost.

sections.title: Simulating the Algorithm on Real Paths
sections.content:
More than a hundred runs of ICMP Echo/Reply cycles were used, most of 512 cycles lasting from several seconds to twenty minutes. Only one packet was in flight at a time to keep stress on the network minimal. The simulated timeout was plotted against each measured delay to show how it handled load changes, glitches and lost packets.

A packet counted as lost if no reply came within thirty seconds. A packet counted as an RTX packet when the computed timeout was below the measured delay, which would cause a superfluous retransmission. Efficiency is the time spent sending good data divided by that time plus lost-packet and RTX-packet time.

Delays were roughly Poisson distributed in a narrow range, with occasional glitches where packets were delayed many times the typical value. After a long well-behaved stretch the algorithm took too long to adapt, inviting superfluous retransmissions and congestion. Most runs had at least one glitch in 512 volleys, and glitches did not correlate well with baseline delay or with packet loss. The FOE host, in London behind a 14.4-Kbps undersea cable and statistical multiplexor, was the hardest case.
sections.eli5: The test showed that sudden slow moments catch the sender off guard, so it resends too soon and makes traffic worse.

sections.title: The Proposed Improvement
sections.content:
Mills suggests using two weights instead of one: F1 when the sample R is less than the estimate E, and F2 when R is at least E, with F1 greater than F2. The estimate then follows upward trends in delay quickly and downward trends slowly. After trials, F1 = 15/16 and F2 = 3/4 with G = 2 gave the best all-around performance.

Compared with the F = 7/8 and G = 2 used in typical implementations, efficiency was better by some ten percent on FOE, ISID and ISIA, by five percent on most paths, and a few percent worse on a couple (FACC, UCL). Varying G gave no clear gain: a larger G makes superfluous retransmissions less likely but increases the delay when packets are lost. Mills compares the scheme to a peak-detector circuit, with G like a squelch threshold.
sections.eli5: React fast when things get slower, and relax slowly when they speed up, like a careful driver who brakes quickly but eases off gradually.
